## Inequality, Household Economies, and Well-being

I am a social psychologist and PhD candidate in Sociology. I study socioeconomic inequality, the economic lives of households, and well-being: how income, wealth, debt, and economic insecurity shape what people experience, the decisions they make, and the opportunities open to them.

I work with quantitative methods and computational social science to find new ways of representing social reality. That means linking surveys with administrative records, turning texts into structured data, and building models that make social mechanisms visible instead of leaving them buried in averages.

My work also has an educational purpose. I build interactive web tools that let broad audiences and public decision-makers explore social problems and how they work, with quality, evidence-based information they can actually use.

Before my doctoral work, I spent a decade in civil society, education, applied policy research, and public writing. That experience is why I care about research that is rigorous and also useful outside the university.

### Core areas

- Socioeconomic inequality and household economic security
- Wealth, debt, and the economic lives of households
- Social psychology of inequality and well-being
- Quantitative methods and computational social science
- Interactive tools for evidence-based public understanding
